title: The House of the Ninth Floor
premise: Urban explorer Tamsin Villalobos breaks into the derelict Halloway House to map a tunnel network that appears on no survey, only to discover the house's ninth floor exists in no blueprint either. When every mirror begins reflecting the rooms one second late, she realizes the delay is not an echo but an invitation — something on the ninth floor is learning to arrive before the present does. As the night stretches toward sunrise, Tamsin uncovers the truth: the house's last owner bargained away his family's memories to keep the ninth floor fed, and the entity now expects her to renew the contract or take its place. She survives by refusing both options — burning the ledger of remembered names — but the price is her own recollection of why she came, leaving her walking out at dawn with the doors counted and no idea what she lost.
about_author: Jonah Pemberton is the pen name of a former building surveyor who spent a decade inspecting condemned properties across the American Northeast. His fiction draws on the floor plans he was never allowed to photograph.

chapters.title: Doors Counted
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. She enters Halloway House at dusk with her survey kit, counting doors out of habit — eleven on the ground floor, though the exterior says ten. The emotional beat is controlled confidence curdling into unease as she logs the discrepancy and decides to stay anyway.

chapters.title: The Tunnel That Isn't
chapters.summary: Tamsin follows a service corridor behind the pantry into a brick tunnel absent from every city survey she's memorized. Her flashlight finds fresh bootprints going in but none coming out. The beat is explorer's thrill giving way to the first real fear: someone else is here, or was seconds ago.

chapters.title: Nine Floors of Eight
chapters.summary: Back inside, Tamsin climbs the main stairwell and counts landings; the eighth floor is followed by another. The ninth-floor door is warm brass, unmarked, locked from the inside. POV stays with Tamsin. Emotional beat: vertigo — the house has grown a room that shouldn't exist.

chapters.title: One Second Late
chapters.summary: In a bathroom mirror, Tamsin notices her reflection lags — she raises her hand, the glass follows a heartbeat behind. She tests every mirror in the house; all are late, and the delay is growing. Beat: rational mind scrambling for explanations while dread settles in like weather.

chapters.title: The Previous Guest
chapters.summary: Tamsin finds a campsite in the library — sleeping bag, dead phone, a journal signed 'M. Okafor.' The journal describes the same lagging mirrors and ends mid-sentence. Beat: grief for a stranger and the cold knowledge that she is following a script already written.

chapters.title: What Was Invited In
chapters.summary: Okafor's journal names the mechanism: the house's owner, Edmund Halloway, invited 'the tenant' in 1974 to preserve his dying wife's memories, paying in the family's own recollections. Tamsin reads by candlelight as footsteps cross the floor above. Beat: horrified understanding — this is a contract, and contracts have terms.

chapters.title: The Ledger of Names
chapters.summary: In the study safe, Tamsin finds a leather ledger listing every person who has entered since 1974, each name struck through except hers and Okafor's. Okafor's entry is half-struck. Beat: the trap snaps shut — she was expected, catalogued, awaited.

chapters.title: Reflections Arriving Early
chapters.summary: The mirrors now show rooms before she enters them — the kitchen, lit, with a figure standing at the counter facing away. When she arrives, it's empty, but the chair is still turning. Beat: time itself is being negotiated, and she is losing the negotiation.

chapters.title: The Tenant Speaks
chapters.summary: Through a hallway mirror, a voice addresses Tamsin — polite, patient, wearing the sound of her mother's tone. It offers her a deal: renew the contract, keep her memories, walk out whole. Beat: temptation rendered intimate; the horror knows exactly what she misses most.

chapters.title: Okafor's Last Entry
chapters.summary: Deciphering water-damaged pages, Tamsin learns Okafor refused the deal and tried to burn the ledger; the journal breaks off at the moment of failure. His half-struck name means the tenant is still collecting him somewhere. Beat: resolve hardening — refusal costs everything, but acceptance costs more.

chapters.title: The Ninth Floor Opens
chapters.summary: The brass door unlocks itself. Inside: a corridor of doors, each opening onto a memory-room staged from Halloway family life — birthdays, funerals, an empty crib. Beat: awe weaponized; the ninth floor is beautiful, and beauty here is bait.

chapters.title: Edmund's Room
chapters.summary: Tamsin enters a recreation of Edmund Halloway's study and meets his recorded confession: he fed the tenant his children's memories one by one until they forgot him, then himself. Beat: pity for the monster's maker and recognition of the theme — power corrupts even love into consumption.

chapters.title: The Price of Survival
chapters.summary: The tenant shows Tamsin her own memories playing in the mirrors — her sister, the accident, the guilt she carries. Renewal would erase the guilt, keep everything else. Beat: the offer becomes almost unbearable; survival has never looked so much like surrender.

chapters.title: Sunrise Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Tamsin calculates hours left and realizes the mirrors aren't lagging anymore — they're synchronized, meaning the tenant has finished learning the present. Beat: ticking-clock panic; the window for any choice is closing faster than she thought.

chapters.title: Half a Name
chapters.summary: She hears Okafor — faint, through the walls, repeating his own name like a man holding onto a rope. Following the voice, she finds him folded into a mirror, aware, unable to leave. Beat: horror crystallized into witness; this is what refusal bought him, and what awaits her.

chapters.title: The Third Option
chapters.summary: Trapped between renewal and replacement, Tamsin re-reads the contract's wording and spots the flaw: the tenant can only hold what is written in the ledger. Unwritten, unremembered, unnamed — nothing to feed on. Beat: hope arriving sideways, earned by attention rather than force.

chapters.title: Burning the Book
chapters.summary: Tamsin takes the ledger to the hearth. The tenant floods the room with her sister's voice, her mother's, begging her to stop. She strikes the match anyway. Beat: climax of will — grief wielded deliberately, the cost accepted before it's paid.

chapters.title: What the Fire Takes
chapters.summary: As pages burn, the house convulses; the ninth floor folds downward through the floors above. But the fire reaches into Tamsin too, taking the memory of why she came — the tunnel, the survey, the reason she explores at all. Beat: victory and loss in the same breath.

chapters.title: Freeing Okafor
chapters.summary: With the contract voided, the mirror holding Okafor cracks. He steps out aged and hollow, remembering nothing but his own name, which he repeats like a prayer. They climb down together. Beat: grim mercy — survival shared, though neither knows what they survived.

chapters.title: Dawn, Doors Counted
chapters.summary: Tamsin exits at first light, counting doors out of habit: ten on the ground floor, correct at last. Okafor walks east without goodbye. She stands in the wet grass trying to remember why her boots are muddy. Beat: quiet devastation — the price paid in full, invisible to its payer.

chapters.title: The Survey
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Tamsin files her tunnel maps and finds a page in her own handwriting she doesn't recall writing: a sketch of a ninth-floor door and the words 'DO NOT COUNT THE DOORS.' Beat: haunting afterthought — some knowledge survives forgetting, and it wants to be read.

chapters.title: One Second Early
chapters.summary: Final chapter, Tamsin's POV. In her apartment mirror, her reflection moves a fraction before she does — just once, just slightly. She turns the glass to the wall and keeps the lights on. Beat: unresolved dread; the tenant learned more than the ledger ever held, and it is patient.
